title: Reverse-Lookup Service Exposed Millions of Photos of People’s Faces
gist: The people-search tool ClarityCheck left more than 9 million image files (roughly 450 GB, including faces of adults, teens, and children) in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket, plus a misconfigured API exposing names, emails, and phone numbers. The incident highlights the structural risk of identity-verification services that depend on collecting sensitive, unchangeable biometric data.

insights.claim: Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler found ClarityCheck left more than 9 million image files—roughly 450 GB including profile images, screenshots, and photos of adults, teenagers, and children—in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket accessible via a URL in the company's public website code.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: A large biometric-data breach at a people-search vendor is a concrete data-governance and litigation risk.

insights.claim: A second misconfiguration let ClarityCheck's website URLs be manipulated so that entering a name returned multiple email addresses, physical addresses, and phone numbers via any consumer browser.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: An API that leaks PII by simple URL manipulation is a low-effort, high-impact exploit path.

insights.claim: Accidental exposures are especially dangerous for sensitive, unchangeable biometric data like face images, and people whose faces were exposed may have had no idea ClarityCheck held their image since the service is designed to identify others.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah Fowler
insights.so_what: Unlike passwords, exposed face data cannot be reset, making biometric breaches permanently exploitable.
insights.quote: you might not have authorization or permission, so people might not know that their image had been dumped into this database

insights.claim: Fowler warns exposed photos are more valuable than ever, enabling a criminal to pick attractive faces and combine them with AI to create catfishing personas, and that an AI bot could crawl the bucket and extract faces for training.
insights.speaker: Jeremiah Fowler
insights.so_what: Leaked biometric data feeds directly into AI-powered fraud and unauthorized model training.

insights.claim: ClarityCheck disputed that the data was 'exposed,' arguing access required knowledge of a specific unindexed URL not discoverable through ordinary use, and that the files included duplicate, cropped, and resized copies, not 9 million unique images.
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: A vendor minimizing a breach by redefining 'exposure' is a red flag for downstream regulatory scrutiny.
insights.quote: We do not accept that data in the temporary storage location was ‘publicly exposed,’ which implies large-scale public access

insights.claim: The security industry and US federal government consider data exposed if it is reachable on the open internet without authentication, whether or not anyone has yet accessed it, per Malwarebytes' Mark Beare.
insights.speaker: Mark Beare
insights.so_what: Establishes the accepted definitional standard that contradicts ClarityCheck's minimization.
insights.quote: A publicly reachable database backup, a misconfigured storage bucket, or credentials sitting in a system that a researcher can reach are all exposures.

insights.claim: The ACLU's Rebecca Williams argues systems relying on highly sensitive personal information to verify individuals will keep carrying these risks even with stronger data minimization, because the model itself depends on collecting sensitive data.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Williams
insights.so_what: Frames the breach risk as inherent to the business model, not a fixable one-off, implicating the whole people-search sector.
insights.quote: the model itself depends on collecting sensitive data

insights.claim: ClarityCheck's face-search returns a report that can include a full name, addresses, location history, public appearances, photos, videos, social media profiles, and 'hidden dating profiles' for a fee, after 'scanning facial landmarks' and 'mapping unique face geometry.'
insights.speaker: Lily Hay Newman
insights.so_what: Details the surveillance capability these services sell, which amplifies the harm when the underlying data leaks.
